title: Linux Systems for Verification
description: Debug-oriented Linux drills: processes, devices, networking tools, and performance hygiene

questions.question: Write a command that lists listening TCP sockets with numeric ports and the owning process (modern iproute2 tool, not netstat).
questions.explanation: ss is the modern socket statistics tool; -lntp shows listening TCP with numeric ports and processes.

questions.scenario: Your SDK test opens /dev/nvidia0 and fails with Permission denied for a non-root CI user.
questions.question: List TWO distinct Linux mechanisms that could be causing this (permissions-related).
questions.modelAnswer: Device node mode/owner/group (udev rules) and missing capabilities or supplementary group membership for the CI user.
questions.explanation: Device access is gated by filesystem permissions/udev groups and often capabilities — both show up constantly in HW/SW labs.

questions.question: What does ethtool primarily help you inspect or change?
options: NIC link modes, offloads, rings/channels, and driver statistics
Git commit graphs across Gerrit repositories
Python package versions inside a virtualenv
questions.explanation: ethtool is the standard Linux interface to NIC driver settings and stats.

questions.question: In one sentence: what is the difference between a Linux process and a thread?
questions.modelAnswer: A process owns an address space/resources; threads are schedulable contexts that can share that address space.
questions.explanation: This distinction matters when debugging concurrency and attributing CPU samples.

questions.question: Write a command to show kernel/driver messages from the kernel ring buffer.
questions.explanation: Driver probes, link flaps, and oopses land in the kernel log.

questions.scenario: Throughput test variance is huge run-to-run on a dual-socket server. IRQs for the NIC mostly land on CPU0. Worker threads float across all cores.
questions.question: Name TWO concrete Linux knobs/techniques you would apply to stabilize results.
questions.modelAnswer: Pin IRQs/queues to specific CPUs and pin worker threads (taskset/cgroups), preferably with NUMA locality in mind.
questions.explanation: IRQ imbalance and scheduler migration are classic sources of noisy networking benchmarks.

questions.question: Why use strace during SDK verification?
options: To record system calls/signals and spot failed opens, ioctls, or permissions
To rewrite kernel modules without rebuilding the running kernel
To raise NIC line rate beyond PHY capability
To step the CPU pipeline cycle-by-cycle like a logic analyzer
questions.explanation: strace reveals the syscall boundary — invaluable when an SDK fails before your app logic runs.

questions.question: Using ethtool, write a command to show which offload features are on/off for nic eth0.
questions.explanation: -k dumps offload features; pair with -K to change them during A/B tests.

questions.question: What does uname -r report, and why do SDK verification matrices care?
questions.modelAnswer: The running kernel release — driver/module ABI and behavior differ across kernels, so you matrix-test.
questions.explanation: Kernel version skew is a top source of “works on my machine” in driver/SDK stacks.

questions.question: What are cgroups primarily for?
options: Limiting and accounting CPU/memory/I/O for groups of processes
Signing RPM packages with a vendor GPG key
Compiling the kernel with a board defconfig
Assigning public IPs exclusively via DHCP
questions.explanation: cgroups underpin containers and reproducible resource limits in CI labs.

questions.question: Give one example Linux capability useful for a packet-capture tool that should not run as full root.
questions.modelAnswer: CAP_NET_RAW (and/or CAP_NET_ADMIN depending on the operations).
questions.explanation: Capabilities split root power — safer test tooling is a leadership-visible quality signal.

questions.question: Write a Python snippet that prints whether a path exists and is readable by the current process (use pathlib or os).
questions.starterCode:
from pathlib import Path
path = Path("/dev/nic_dbg")
questions.modelAnswer: print(path.exists())  # plus os.access(path, os.R_OK) for readability
questions.explanation: Preflight checks in harnesses catch environment issues before expensive suites run.

followUpQuestions.question: Which tool traces system calls of a process?
Command to show NIC offloads for eth0?
CPU pinning is primarily used to…
options: Encrypt all packets with IPsec automatically
Replace TCP with UDP for every socket
followUpQuestions.explanation: Pinning reduces scheduler noise and helps NUMA/IRQ locality.

followUpQuestions.question: Where do you often look first for driver probe failures?
followUpQuestions.explanation: Driver messages land in the kernel log.

followUpQuestions.question: What do cgroups control?
followUpQuestions.explanation: cgroups limit and account process-group resources.

Linux Systems for Verification — Study Guide

For the full interactive course, open this section’s Learn path (Basics → Advanced → Expert). Every important command is explained flag-by-flag there.

Level map

  • Basics: Users, devices, sockets, and kernel messages
  • Advanced: strace, ethtool, modules, IRQ imbalance
  • Expert: cgroups, capabilities, perf, reproducible labs

Free resources

  • Linux Journey — Gentle free path through Linux fundamentals.
  • ss(8) — Socket statistics reference.
  • ethtool(8) — NIC settings & stats flags.

tutorial.intro: Build Linux lab fluency: permissions, sockets, NIC tooling, logs, and performance isolation — every command explained.

levels.title: Basics
levels.tagline: Users, devices, sockets, and kernel messages
levels.html:
Goal: stop treating Linux as a black box. Know who you are, what you can open, and where errors land.

1. Who am I on this machine?

id
id
Print your user ID (uid), primary group (gid), and supplementary groups.
groups
groups
Quick list of group names — important for /dev access (e.g. dialout, docker, render).
Why groups matter for SDKs

Many device nodes are mode 660 root:somegroup. If your CI user is not in somegroup, open() returns EACCES — the SDK looks “broken” but the environment is wrong.

2. Inspect a device node

ls -l /dev/nvidia0
ls -l
Long listing: permissions, owner, group, name.
/dev/nvidia0
Example char device — replace with your NIC/USB/GPU node.

Read crw-rw---- 1 root video as: character device; owner root can rw; group video can rw; others nothing.

3. Listening ports & processes

ss -lntp
ss
Show socket state (connections and listeners).
-l
Listening only.
-n
Numeric addresses/ports.
-t
TCP.
-p
Process that owns the socket.
ss -lunp
-u
UDP instead of TCP — same idea for datagram listeners.

4. Kernel/driver messages

dmesg -T | tail -50
dmesg
Print the kernel ring buffer (driver probes, link flaps, oopses).
-T
Human-readable timestamps.
tail -50
Only the last 50 lines for a quick look.
journalctl -k -b --no-pager | tail -50
journalctl
systemd journal query tool.
-k
Kernel messages only.
-b
This boot only.
--no-pager
Print to stdout (CI-friendly).
First place for “driver didn’t load”

Search dmesg/journal for the module/NIC name right after failure. Userspace logs often never see the real error.

5. Processes vs threads (interview crispness)

A process owns an address space and resources (FDs, etc.). Threads are schedulable execution contexts that can share that address space. SDK bugs that appear only under load are often thread-safety bugs.

levels.title: Advanced
levels.html:
1. strace: watch syscalls fail in real time

strace -f -o /tmp/sdk.strace ./your_test
strace
Trace system calls and signals of a program.
-f
Follow children/threads (critical for multi-process tests).
-o /tmp/sdk.strace
Write output to a file (easier to search).
./your_test
The command you are debugging.
strace -e openat,ioctl,connect ./your_test
-e openat,ioctl,connect
Only show these syscalls — less noise when you already suspect device/network.
What to look for

openat(...)= -1 EACCES / ENOENT, ioctl failures, connect ETIMEDOUT/ECONNREFUSED. Those errno values are the diagnosis.

2. ethtool deep dive

ethtool eth0
ethtool eth0
Link settings: speed, duplex, auto-neg, link detected.
ethtool -k eth0
-k
Offload features list (checksum/TSO/GRO…).
ethtool -S eth0 | egrep -i "err|drop|disc|miss"
-S
Driver stats dump.
egrep ...
Filter to error/drop-like counters quickly.
sudo ethtool -K eth0 tso off
-K ... tso off
Disable one offload for A/B correctness testing.

3. Kernel modules

uname -r
uname -r
Running kernel release — modules must match this ABI.
lsmod | head
lsmod
List loaded kernel modules.
modinfo
modinfo
Show module path, version, parameters, firmware deps.

4. IRQ / CPU imbalance

grep eth0 /proc/interrupts
/proc/interrupts
Per-CPU interrupt counters.
grep eth0
NIC IRQs only — if one CPU column dominates, perf numbers are suspect.
taskset -c 2-5 ./throughput_test
taskset
Launch a process bound to specific CPUs.
-c 2-5
Allow CPUs 2 through 5 only.
./throughput_test
Your benchmark binary.

levels.title: Expert
levels.html:
1. Capabilities instead of root

man 7 capabilities
capabilities(7)
Documents CAP_* privileges that split “root powers”.

Examples: CAP_NET_RAW for sniffing, CAP_NET_ADMIN for interface config. Grant only what the tool needs.

sudo setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin+ep /usr/local/bin/lab-tool
setcap
Attach capability bits to a binary.
cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin+ep
Effective+permitted caps for network admin/raw.

2. cgroups (why containers isolate resources)

cgroups limit/account CPU, memory, I/O for process groups. CI fairness and reproducible limits depend on them.

3. perf quick start

perf top
perf top
Live CPU profile: which functions burn samples right now.
perf record -g ./benchmark && perf report
perf record -g
Record samples with call-graph.
./benchmark
Workload under test.
perf report
Interactive report of hot paths.

4. Ship a preflight script (professional bar)

  • Check uname -r, driver/module loaded, device node permissions
  • Check link up via ethtool
  • Print versions into CI artifacts
  • Fail early with a clear message
Line that sounds experienced

“We productized lab preflight — false failures from permissions/driver skew dropped dramatically.”
